name: Mexico City
info: Mexico City is the capital and largest city of Mexico, in the Valley of Mexico on the central plateau, built after 1521 on the ruins of the Mexica city of Tenochtitlan and since then a viceregal, imperial and republican capital.

facts.founded: Founded as Tenochtitlan by the Mexica in 1325 or 1327, on an island in Lake Texcoco; the Spanish razed it in 1521 and Hernán Cortés founded the Spanish colonial capital on the site.
facts.where: In the Valley of Mexico, a basin on the high plateaus of south-central Mexico, at an altitude of about 2,240 metres, on the bed of the former Lake Texcoco.
facts.known: The Mexica city of Tenochtitlan and its siege and destruction in 1521; the capital of New Spain; the Zócalo and the Metropolitan Cathedral; the Desagüe, the long effort to drain the valley; the capital of independent Mexico; the muralists; the earthquake of 1985
facts.today: Mexico City, officially Ciudad de México or CDMX since 2016, is the capital and largest city of Mexico and is divided into 16 boroughs.

t: The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco in 1325 or 1327, and in 1521 Spanish forces and their Indigenous allies besieged and razed it, and Cuauhtémoc surrendered in August.

Cortés founded the Spanish capital on the ruins, and for three centuries Mexico City was the seat of the viceroyalty of New Spain, its archbishopric and its merchants, and afterwards the capital of independent Mexico.

The city sat on a lake bed with no natural outlet, so floods led to a drainage works begun in 1607 and finished under Porfirio Díaz, while later growth overflowed the Federal District and the soft clay began to sink.
dyk: The colonial city was built on the saturated clay of the former lake bed, and since the beginning of the 20th century it has sunk as much as nine metres in some areas and continues to sink almost 50 centimetres a year.
ev: The Mexica found Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco, a date some sources give as 1327
Cuauhtémoc surrenders after the three-month siege and Tenochtitlan is razed, and Cortés refounds the city as Mexico
Thousands of Indigenous workers are drafted to dig the first Desagüe, the drainage ditch and tunnel
The Army of the Three Guarantees enters the city and Mexico is declared independent
United States troops under Winfield Scott take the city after the battles of Molino del Rey and Chapultepec
The Decena Trágica ends with the coup of Victoriano Huerta and the killing of Francisco Madero
An earthquake of magnitude 8.1 collapses hundreds of buildings
The city elects its mayor for the first time since 1928

sections.origins:
The city stands in the Valley of Mexico, a basin in the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt on the high plateaus of south-central Mexico. The valley has no natural drainage outlet, and for most of its history the site lay in Lake Texcoco, a system of interconnected salt and freshwater lakes. The oldest signs of human occupation in the area are those of the Peñón woman, whom a 2003 study dated to 12,700 years ago. After the fall of the Toltec capital of Tollan, large migrations of Nahuatl-speaking peoples entered the valley and founded city-states around the lake. The Mexica were the last wave, and the peoples already there resisted their coming.

The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan on an island on the western side of the lake in 1325 or 1327. Their own story is that the god Huitzilopochtli led them there after a long migration and marked the place with an eagle perched on a prickly pear cactus, to which later versions add a snake in its beak. Three codices place the founding in 1325, and Carlos de Sigüenza y Góngora gives the day 18 July 1327. A group left the island after internal strife and set up a monarchy of its own at Tlatelolco, which Tenochtitlan later conquered and absorbed. From 1430 the Mexica and their allies of Texcoco and Tlacopan conquered the Valley of Mexico and took tribute from the peoples who had resisted them. Tenochtitlan was laid out with streets and canals on the cardinal directions, in four districts, and it roughly corresponds to the historic centre of the present city.
sections.growth:
Tenochtitlan is estimated to have held at least 100,000 and perhaps as many as 200,000 people when the Spaniards first saw it in 1519. The Spanish city that replaced it grew as the seat of power. Cortés took over the old palaces of Axayacatl and Moctezuma for his own houses on the main square, later called the Plaza Mayor or Zócalo,. The Franciscan friar Toribio de Benavente Motolinia counted the rebuilding of the city among the afflictions of the early years, with many workers killed by falling beams or in the tearing down of old buildings. By the 1530s Mexico City had jurisdiction over other town councils of New Spain. The University of Mexico was founded in 1553 and the merchants' guild, the consulado, in 1594, and from the late 1560s until 1813 the Manila galleon carried silver from Acapulco to Manila in exchange for Chinese silks and porcelain.

In the later 18th century nobles who had made fortunes in mining or on haciendas elsewhere spent them in the capital on mansions, which gave the city its nickname of the City of Palaces. An estimate for 1689 was 57,000, and the census of Viceroy Revillagigedo in 1790 counted 112,926 residents. In the 19th century the city spread by extending its rectangular grid and in 1865 Maximilian had a wide avenue laid out, later the Paseo de la Reforma. Under Porfirio Díaz, from 1876, the city gained better roads, schools and transport. The city had about 500,000 people in 1900 and then spread west and south, and between 1960 and 1980 its population more than doubled to 8,831,079, overflowing the boundaries of the Federal District.
sections.rulers:
Tenochtitlan was ruled by its tlatoani, Moctezuma being its ruler when the Spaniards arrived. After the siege of 1521 Cortés first settled at Coyoacán and made the new Spanish capital on the island, and although he did not set up a territory under his own rule and stayed loyal to Charles V, the emperor did not appoint him governor of New Spain. The viceroyalty of New Spain was seated in the city, as were the Audiencia and the archbishopric. Two Indigenous sections, San Juan Tenochtitlan and Santiago Tlatelolco, were governed by Nahua governors and councils, and the city was designated a city of Spaniards.

On 21 September 1821 Agustín de Iturbide's Army of the Three Guarantees entered the city, and independence was declared on 27 September. Iturbide was crowned emperor in the cathedral on 21 July 1822 and abdicated in the spring of 1823, after which Mexico became a republic. The constitution of 1824 made Mexico City the capital, and Congress set apart a federal district around the Zócalo on 18 November 1824. United States forces occupied the city after 1847. In the Reform War of 1857 to 1861 the Liberals governed from Veracruz and the Conservatives from the capital, until Benito Juárez moved his government there. Maximilian ruled the Second Mexican Empire from 1864 to 1867, and Porfirio Díaz governed Mexico from 1876 to 1910. The city lost its elected mayor and council in 1928, when the president began to appoint the mayor, and Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas was elected in 1997. On 29 January 2016 the Federal District was renamed Ciudad de México.
sections.life:
After the conquest Spaniards lived in the traza around the Zócalo, in orderly streets, and Indigenous people lived in sections outside it, though Indigenous traders used the Zócalo and the Spanish effort to keep the areas apart was hard to enforce. The 1793 count of the city, which omits officials, listed 50,371 Spaniards (48.1 per cent), 25,603 Indians (24.4 per cent), 19,357 mestizos, 7,094 mulattos and 2,335 Europeans. It had the largest concentration of people of Spanish descent and of mixed ancestry in the colony. The city also held many poor people. The Nacional Monte de Piedad, a pawnshop giving interest-free small loans, was set up in 1777 by the Count of Regla, and the Royal Cigar Factory gave thousands of jobs to the urban poor, women among them. Revillagigedo cleared pulque stalls and animals from the Plaza Mayor, paved and lit it, and had the entrance of the Alameda guarded so that poorly clad people could not enter.

The city was the centre of religious power. The cult of the Virgin of Guadalupe is said to have originated in a vision at Tepeyac Hill in 1531, and Bernardino de Sahagún suspected it of continuing the Aztec cult of Tonantzin. The Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco is recognised as the first European school of higher learning in the Americas. After the Mexican Revolution muralism began in the city, and works by Orozco, Siqueiros and Diego Rivera stand in the National Palace and the Palacio de Bellas Artes. Nahuatl, Otomi, Mixtec, Zapotec and Mazahua are the Indigenous languages with most speakers there today.
sections.crises:
The conquest was a siege. Cortés entered Tenochtitlan on 8 November 1519, was received by Moctezuma and held him under house arrest. While Cortés was away, Pedro de Alvarado ordered a massacre during the spring festival of Huitzilopochtli. Moctezuma was wounded by stones and arrows from his own people and died soon after; whether the Spanish killed him is not known. On the night of 30 June 1520, La Noche Triste, the Mexica drove the Spaniards and Tlaxcalans out, killing at least 600 Spaniards. Cortés besieged the city from May 1521. For three months it suffered from lack of food and water and from disease brought by the Europeans, and Spanish forces and their allies fought through it street by street until Cuauhtémoc surrendered in August 1521. The dikes were destroyed and Tenochtitlan was razed.

The lake caused floods, and from 1607 thousands of Indigenous people were drafted to dig the Desagüe. In 1642 the Inquisition arrested 150 crypto-Jews, and on 11 April 1649 twelve were burned after being strangled and one alive. Riots in 1624 and 1692 ousted a viceroy and burned the residences of the archbishop and the viceroy. In September 1847 United States troops took the city. During the Decena Trágica of February 1913 the centre was shelled and Madero was shot after Huerta's coup. Government troops killed an unknown number of protesting students at Tlatelolco in 1968, and the 1985 earthquake collapsed 412 buildings and killed about 10,000 people, a figure in dispute.
sections.legacy:
The Zócalo, the old Aztec ceremonial centre, became the Plaza Mayor of the colony and is now the central square of the nation, with the Metropolitan Cathedral on one side. Many colonial buildings and palaces remain in the historic centre and serve as government buildings and museums. The Ciudad Universitaria of the National Autonomous University, built from 1950 to 1953 with murals by Rivera and Siqueiros, was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007, and the Metro opened its first line in 1969. The soft clay of the former lake bed is collapsing as groundwater is over-extracted, and the city has sunk as much as nine metres in some areas since the start of the 20th century. From the 1940s a freeze on rents, repealed in 1998, left the centre's buildings to decay, and the area lost about 100,000 residents before efforts to restore it began in the early 2000s.

Mexico City is today the capital and largest city of Mexico, and about 9.2 million people live in the city proper and about 21.8 million in Greater Mexico City, which extends into the State of Mexico and Hidalgo. Its centre sits on the site of Tenochtitlan, whose name endured in the Indigenous section of San Juan Tenochtitlan and in the eagle and cactus at the centre of the Mexican flag.

summary: Mexico City is the capital of Mexico, in the Valley of Mexico. The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan there in 1325 or 1327, and after Spanish forces and their allies razed it in 1521 Cortés built the colonial capital of New Spain on its ruins. It became the capital of independent Mexico in 1821.
notes: FOUNDING DATE: city article says 1325 or 1327; history article gives three codices for 1325 and Sigüenza y Góngora for 18 July 1327. start = 1325, circa true; both stated in the text.

TENOCHTITLAN POPULATION: the history article's lead says at least 100,000 and perhaps 200,000 in 1519, but its founding section says 150,000 perhaps 200,000 for the early 16th century. I gave only the lead's hedge, for 1519.
CITY OF PALACES: the city article attributes the nickname to Humboldt; the history article says Latrobe coined it and the Humboldt attribution is erroneous. I used the nickname with no attribution.

FIRST VICEROY: the two articles say he arrived fourteen years later (history: after Cortés's grant of 1528-30, which would be c. 1542-44; city: fourteen years after the conquest, 1535). Disagree, so no date or name given.

CHURUBUSCO: city article dates it 8 August (probably an error for September); left out. The battle for the city is 8 to 15 September 1847 in the city article; I wrote only September 1847. Mexican losses of 10,000 at Churubusco left out.

Moctezuma's death: the history article says it is unknown whether his injuries or the Spanish killed him; I kept that. The 'Quetzalcoatl prophecy' is described by the history article as heavily criticised by historians; left out.

La Noche Triste: 30 June 1520 from the city article. Spanish dead 'at least 600 (some estimates over 1,000)'; I gave 'at least 600'. Tlaxcalan loss 'probably several thousand'. Cuitláhuac (city article only) not mentioned.

DESTRUCTION: city article: 'practically razed'; history: 'besieged and razed'. I wrote 'razed' in the text and takeaway; the editor may want 'practically razed'. The dikes were destroyed 'during the siege' (city article).

Desagüe: history says 4,500 drafted in 1607 for an 8-mile ditch and tunnel, 3,000 in 1608; 'finished under Díaz' (the engineering project 'successfully finished', 'the cycle of flooding finally ended') is the history article's account; the city article says only that drainage began in the 17th century.

Mayor: history says the elected mayor and council were lost in 1928 and the mayor appointed by the president; elections restored by the 1990s reforms; Cárdenas elected 1997. 'Sixteen boroughs' and the 2016 renaming from the city article.

1793 census (history article): the figures are those of Valdés from the 1790 census counted in 1793 (104,760 residents excluding 8,166 officials); I gave the five categories. The 1790 Revillagigedo count is 112,926. The two differ in what they include.

Huerta: the history says Madero and Pino Suárez were 'shot and killed' by armed men on the way to Lecumberri; city says 'murdered'. Shelling of the centre and civilian casualties from the city article.
1968: 'an unknown number of protesting students' killed by government troops (history) at Tlatelolco; I wrote 'soldiers'. The 'Halcones' repression of 1971 left out.
1985: 412 collapsed, 3,124 seriously damaged, about 10,000 deaths 'most-often cited' (in dispute); damage $3-4 billion left out. Magnitude 8.1.
Population today: city proper 9,209,944 and Greater Mexico City 21,804,515 (2020 census); given as rounded figures with no year, per the guide.

Left out: tourism, rankings and GDP, transport, sports, pollution detail, the present government's policies, the 2020 mammoth find, climate, cuisine, the climate of the city and the Nicknames of residents.
The Aztec city is told briefly in origins and growth; the profile of Tenochtitlan exists separately. 'Mexica' used for the people, 'Aztec' as the articles use it for the empire and ceremonial centre.
Smallpox: the profile does not state it as a cause; the history article calls the 1520 epidemic a factor in the conquest, which the siege passage's 'disease brought by the Europeans' follows.
TAKEAWAY 1 / crises: 'razed' follows the history article's lead ('besieged and razed'); the city article says 'practically razed'.
